one_liner: Arm's reference ASTC texture compressor (CLI plus C/C++ library); 2.x and later are 2-3.5x faster than its own 1.7 series.
what_it_does: astcenc compresses LDR and HDR images (2D and 3D, every ASTC block size from 4x4 to 12x12 and the 3D sizes) to ASTC for OpenGL ES, Vulkan and Metal GPUs, and decompresses them back. It ships as a CLI tool (-cl/-cs/-ch/-cH compress, -d* decompress, -t* round-trip with PSNR) and as a core codec library behind astcenc.h: config_init with a quality preset, context_alloc, then astcenc_compress_image on caller-owned memory buffers. Six presets (-fastest, -fast, -medium, -thorough, -verythorough, -exhaustive) set the time/quality point.
how_it_is_fast: The 2.0 rewrite added a SIMD abstraction (vfloat4/vint4/vfloat8) with SSE2, SSE4.1, AVX2 and later NEON, SVE and RISC-V V backends, replacing 1.7's scalar code. Partition search runs k-means on the block's texels, ranks all 1024 hash-generated partitionings by how many texels disagree with that clustering, and gives the detailed endpoint and weight search only the top N candidates. Per-preset tuning tables (astcenc_entry.cpp) cap block modes, partition indices and refinement passes, and dB-target and correlation early-outs skip 2-plane and 3/4-partition trials once a good enough encoding is found. 4.x added in-register SIMD permutes for small tables, deferred weight and color packing, and a narrower search for later trials.
when_to_use: Offline asset pipelines that must produce ASTC for mobile or Apple GPUs, especially block sizes above 8x8, HDR (-ch/-cH) or 3D textures, which narrower ASTC encoders do not cover.
Quality-sensitive content (normal maps, mask maps, UI) where -medium or -thorough quality matters more than encode time.
Many-core build machines: one image can be split across N caller threads, and since 5.4.0 several contexts with the same config can share read-only tables when you run one image per thread.
Builds that need identical output on every platform: invariant builds (the default) give bit-exact results across compilers and ISAs.
Arm64 build hosts: NEON and SVE 128/256 backends are first-class, with prebuilt Linux Arm64 binaries since 5.2.0.
when_not_to_use: Latency-bound runtime encoding of 2D LDR photos: Arm's own astcenc 3.1 blog (search snippet only, page blocked) says ISPC TexComp can be up to 3x faster at quality similar to -fast, though worse on normal and mask maps. A Chalmers thesis snippet claims up to 44x for Intel's encoder at the same quality, against an unstated, probably older astcenc.
Non-ASTC targets (BC1-BC7, ETC1/ETC2): astcenc encodes ASTC only.

Distributing one binary for unknown x86 CPUs: the core library does no runtime ISA dispatch (issue #672, open, asks for it), so you ship SSE2/SSE4.1/AVX2 variants and choose one yourself. macOS gets a universal binary.
Data that needs 1-bit punch-through alpha, signed values (as in BC6H signed) or two-plane .rg sampling like BC5: Encoding.md says ASTC has no direct equivalent.
Choosing a speed winner over rival encoders: the only measured speedup is against astcenc's own 1.7 release, so this entry gives no evidence against ISPC, GPU or other ASTC encoders.

integration.form: static lib (CMake core codec library, optional shared lib via ASTCENC_SHAREDLIB) plus CLI tool
integration.dependencies: none for the core codec; the CLI bundles stb_image, Wuffs and TinyEXR; unit tests use a googletest submodule
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 14), CMake 3.15+; tested with Clang 9+, Visual Studio 2019+ (ClangCL recommended) and Xcode 14+; astcenc.h is C-compatible since 5.4.0
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE2; SSE4.1+POPCNT; AVX2+POPCNT+F16C), aarch64 (NEON, SVE 128-bit, SVE 256-bit), RISC-V V at VLEN=256 through the NONE/NATIVE build, portable reference C (big-endian with ASTCENC_BIG_ENDIAN=ON); Windows, Linux, macOS, Android unofficial
integration.thread_safety: One context per image stream. To split one image across threads, allocate the context with thread_count N and call astcenc_compress_image once per thread with distinct thread_index; the caller creates the threads and calls compress_reset between images. Contexts with the same config can share read-only tables (5.4.0+). astcenc_compress_cancel (5.2.0+) stops an in-flight compression.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same ASTC output format as 1.7, but the 2.0 CLI is not command-line compatible with 1.7, and the library API broke between minor releases until 5.4.0 (semantic versioning since then)

gotchas: No runtime ISA check in the core library: an AVX2 or SVE-256 build on a CPU without that ISA faults, so the caller must check, as astcenccli_entry.cpp does. SVE builds must match the host vector length.

Invariance is on by default and costs speed. ASTCENC_INVARIANCE=OFF enables -ffp-contract=fast (and -mfma on AVX2) for up to 5-20% more speed at up to 0.2 dB lower quality, but output then differs across compilers and platforms. Building.md also says Clang builds are about 15% faster than GCC builds.

If textures are sampled with the decode_unorm8 extension, compress with -decode_unorm8 or ASTCENC_FLG_USE_DECODE_UNORM8 to get the right rounding. Contexts made with ASTCENC_FLG_SELF_DECOMPRESS_ONLY can return magenta error blocks when decoding images from other encoders or configurations.

Preset names do not mean equal effort across major versions (4.2 retuned -exhaustive to 3x slower and added -verythorough; 4.6 pruned -medium and -thorough again), and 5.7.0 removed the -repeats benchmarking option. Re-measure on your content when upgrading.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick astcenc over refreshed-astc-encoder, a fork of the 2015-era code measured only against old Arm binaries, for anything current. Pick it over the ISPC kernels behind intel-tex-rs-2 when you need HDR, 3D, block sizes above 8x8 or the highest-quality presets; bc7e, bc7enc, etcpak, Goofy and ICBC target BCn/ETC, not ASTC.
verified_claims_summary: Arm's changelog charts (i5-9600K at 4.2 GHz, 6 threads) show astcenc-avx2 2.0 coding about 2-3x faster than astcenc 1.7 at -thorough and mostly 2-3.5x at -medium and -fast, with PSNR mostly within 0.2 dB and one -3.6 dB -fast grayscale outlier; 4.0 is about 1.17-1.74x over 3.7 at -thorough. The baseline is the project's own 1.7: its stock Makefile builds scalar code with -O3 -msse2, against 2.0's -O3 -flto -mavx2 -mpopcnt, so part of the gain is ISA and LTO. No compiler is stated for either side, and no rival encoder is timed.
status_note: Actively maintained by Arm (5.7.0 in August 2026, last commit 2026-08-29), Apache-2.0, fuzzed in OSS-Fuzz; main is the development branch, so production users should pin a release tag.
measurement_notes: Code behind the charts, read this session: the 2.0-tag harness (Test/testlib/encoder.py, class Encoder1x) runs a 1.7 binary from an untracked ./Binaries/1.7/ directory, so its build is not recorded, and parses 1.7's own 'Elapsed time ... coding time' output, while 2.x reports 'Coding time'. That the two timers cover the same work is not documented. At tag 3.7 the Encoder1_7 wrapper parses 2.x-style 'Total time:/Coding time:' lines with the comment 'Pattern match on a new pattern for a 2.1 compatible variant', which implies a locally modified 1.7 binary, and it maps -fastest to -fast. Every harness keeps the best of N repeats. Docs/Testing.md says the reference data was measured at 4.3 GHz, while the changelogs say 4.2 GHz. No correctness bug that would inflate the speed numbers was found. Past encoder bugs (4.2.0 incorrect blue-contract endpoints for RGB/RGBA base+offset encodings; 4.7.0 decoder rounding that did not follow the Khronos spec, LSB flips) affect quality figures, not timing. Tier C stands.
